crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
children.blurb: Retrieval-grounded legal research covers the use of AI systems that answer legal questions by first retrieving relevant passages from primary and secondary sources, then generating a response tied to those passages.

children.name: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
children.blurb: Adversarial statutory interpretation is the practice of using computational tools to identify competing readings of a statute, test how courts might resolve ambiguity, and map the interpretive moves available to each side in litigation.

children.name: Brief Drafting with Machine Assistance
children.blurb: Brief drafting with machine assistance covers the use of AI tools to help lawyers prepare motions, briefs, memoranda, and other court filings.

children.name: Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking
children.blurb: Citation auditing and good law checking is the process of verifying that every authority cited in a legal document remains valid, has not been overruled or reversed, and still supports the proposition for which it is cited.

children.name: Jurisdictional Anomalies and Local Codes
children.blurb: This page covers the uneven patchwork of state, county, and municipal rules that apply to artificial intelligence, where definitions, enforcement dates, and obligations differ from one locality to the next.

sections.body: Legal research and case strategy now uses machine assistance to search case law, statutes, and local codes, then to draft and check legal documents. Retrieval grounded systems pull exact passages from legal databases instead of generating text from memory alone. Adversarial statutory reading tools compare a proposed interpretation against counterarguments drawn from precedent and legislative history. Brief drafting assistants turn an attorney's notes and retrieved sources into a structured first draft. Citation auditing software flags cases that have been overruled, questioned, or distinguished, and jurisdictional tools identify where a local rule departs from a state or federal norm. The site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which reflects the volume of material these systems must search.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The most reliable work is retrieval and citation checking, where a system can match a query to a specific passage and report subsequent negative treatment. Drafting assistance is useful for organizing arguments and producing neutral summaries, but it does not reliably handle novel legal theories or subtle policy judgments. Adversarial statutory interpretation remains experimental because it can miss implied repeals, context dependent definitions, and judicial silence. Jurisdictional anomaly detection is limited by the uneven quality of local code data, and the 6,895 state AI bills tracked on this site change faster than any training set can absorb. No current system can certify that a brief is correct, and every output still requires a lawyer's review.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader would start with Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research to understand how a query becomes a set of sourced passages and why grounding matters. Adversarial Statutory Interpretation then shows how to test a reading against opposing arguments before committing to it. Brief Drafting with Machine Assistance takes those tested readings and turns them into a working document, while Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking verifies that every cited authority still supports the proposition. Jurisdictional Anomalies and Local Codes is the final check for cases where a general rule breaks down, such as local ordinances, tribal codes, or state specific definitions that a national database may miss.
